text:
Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

#India: COURT DENIES KETAN PAREKH PERMISSION FOR 91-DAY FOREIGN HOLIDAY

A special securities court in Mumbai has rejected former stockbroker Ketan Parekh's request to travel to nine countries for a three-month family vacation.

Parekh, whose name became associated with India's major 2000–2001 stock market scandal, sought permission to visit Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Switzerland between December 20, 2026, and March 20, 2027.

At a hearing on November 20, Special SEBI Judge R. M. Jadhav ruled that granting unrestricted permission for such an extended period would not serve India's national or economic interests.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) opposed the application, alleging that Parekh had previously misused permission to travel abroad and had engaged in further securities-related misconduct involving confidential market information.

SEBI also raised concerns over an outstanding order concerning ₹27 crore in alleged unlawful gains.

The court acknowledged the right to travel abroad but concluded that the risks associated with a 91-day absence justified refusing this particular request.

The ruling does not determine liability in the ongoing securities proceedings.

These include the handles of https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, @internetfreedom, @geoblockedindia, and posts from the said organisations and other users. A separate notification identified five (5) URLs concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X account and our posts.

The requests relate to posts discussing legal notices received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). They also include posts by users who commented on or reshared these posts, as well as other posts by @geoblockedindia documenting instances of digital censorship.

Chain of Events

1. On 29 October 2026, when https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia (collectively “Organisations”) received a legal notice from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the RSS. The notice took objection to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's Free Speech Tracker, which documents instances of censorship and online content restrictions and account takedowns in India. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and IFF raised concerns about the authenticity of the notice, which did not carry an official letterhead or identify an authorised signatory.

2. On 1 November 2026, the Organisations received another notice from the same advocate. This notice stated that the matter had been transferred to the RSS's legal and advocacy wing, the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, and referred to complaints allegedly filed in different states.

3. On the same day, X informed https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 that it had received a request from the “Indian Police” alleging that a post discussing the legal notice violated Indian law. However, this notification did not identify the requesting law enforcement agency, statutory provisions invoked, or provide a copy of the underlying order or request. The post remains accessible on X at the time of writing.

4. On 3 November 2026, X communicated further directions from Delhi Police covering 42 URLs, including the URL for https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s account itself. In the attached notices, the first notice refers to Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 which deals with the offence of criminal defamation as the legal basis. The second notice refers to Section 356 of BNS and Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology Rules 2021, which deal with intermediary liability and due diligence of intermediaries as the legal basis. The grounds cited for the takedown requests concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X handle and posts include hate speech, defamation of RSS, and safety/security.

Takedown requests targeting https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's handle threaten its public service work

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's X handle is an important public-facing channel through which it disseminates the organisation's ongoing work to the general public. It is through https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 social media handles that users who face digital rights violation and online harms reach out to us for pro bono legal services. Through the handle we publish legal and policy analysis, document instances of censorship, raise awareness about digital rights violations, and communicate such information with the public including journalists, researchers, civil society organisations among others. It also serves as a channel for sharing developments concerning internet shutdowns, content restrictions, account takedowns and other violations of digital rights and for providing important assistance, through RightsLine, to citizens facing online harms ranging from gender based violence and harassment  to cyberfraud. 

A direction seeking the takedown of an organisation’s entire account, rather than addressing specific content through a transparent and legally established process, would have consequences far beyond the posts that have been identified. It would also deprive the public of an established and credible source of information on digital rights and the exercise of fundamental freedoms online.

The request to restrict https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s entire X handle, rather than identifying and seeking the removal of specific allegedly unlawful content does not meet the necessity and proportionality standards. The right to freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution extends to disseminate information, circulate ideas and reach an audience.  Restrictions on fundamental freedoms must not be arbitrary or excessive and must not go beyond what is necessary to achieve their legitimate objective (Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1951 SC 118). Any restriction on an organisation's established channel of communication must therefore be assessed in light of its wider impact on the organisation's ability to exercise its rights and the public's corresponding right to receive information.

Further, the reliance on Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, raises questions to whether intermediary liability provisions are being used as an independent mechanism for restricting online speech, potentially bypassing the procedural safeguards prescribed under Section 69A of the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b), clarifying that an intermediary's obligation to remove or disable access to content must arise from a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency, and that such orders or notifications must strictly conform to the grounds enumerated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Section 79(3)(b), which forms part of the intermediary safe-harbour framework, cannot be treated as an unrestricted or independent source of blocking power or used to circumvent the safeguards governing restrictions on online information.

It is also pertinent to note that https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors, W.P.(C) 7650/2025 has also challenged the constitutional legality of the notification issued by Lieutenant Governor (LG) which empowers the Delhi Police to issue takedown orders for removal of online content from social media. The matter is currently pending in the Delhi High Court.

Documenting censorship is not facilitating circumvention

The Free Speech Tracker is an initiative to document instances of censorship in India. Its purpose is to make censorship visible, identify patterns in content moderation and provide the public with information about restrictions affecting online expression.

Documenting a restriction does not amount to endorsing the restricted content, facilitating access to it or encouraging circumvention of the law. Over the last few months, we have seen an unprecedented number of online content restrictions happening in India, and in the absence of adequate transparency from the government and platforms about the nature, extent and legal basis of these restrictions, we wanted to document these instances in a manner that is informative to the general public. Freedom of expression encompasses not only the right to publish and disseminate information but also the right to question restrictions on speech, seek accountability and scrutinise decisions affecting public discourse.

Independent civil society organisations like ours play an important role in documenting these developments and ensuring that restrictions on online expression do not go unnoticed. Such takedown requests risk creating a chilling effect on public-interest advocacy and may discourage individuals from discussing or questioning instances of censorship.

Irregularities in notice received

The first notice received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 from X, pertains to this post. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of ‘safety/security; defamation; and other’. Furthermore, the notice states that the post is “defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under the Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).” Criminal defamation under Section 356 of the BNS, 2023, is a non-cognizable offence and therefore, requires a court order for the police to initiate action.

The second notice received, pertains to a list of 42 posts and accounts. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of “Hate speech; safety/security; defamation; enforcement of court order; and other’. The posts published by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 did not contain any defamatory statements or allegations against RSS, as it was purely factual reporting based on information relating to the notice received by the Organisations on 29 October 2026.

Furthermore, criminal defamation is a non-cognizable offence which requires a court order for the police to initiate action. The Delhi Police is not empowered to issue a content takedown order for such offence via the Sahyog Portal in the absence of such an order. While the notice mentions enforcement of a court order as one of the grounds, no such court order is cited or made available in the notice. Additionally, the notice does not identify a legal basis or statutory provision for the offences of hate speech or safety/security. The notice also relies on Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and states that action must be taken by X within 3 hours.

Therefore, in light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 condemns the takedown request issued by the Delhi Police and maintains that they are unlawful, disproportionate and violative of the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police and the concerned authorities to immediately withdraw these requests. If there exists any relevant court order directing the removal of the content, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police to provide copies of said order to the Organisations (https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF, and @geoblockedindia) posthaste. 

We stand in solidarity with all individuals and organisations affected by these takedown requests and reaffirm our commitment to defending their right to speak, document and question restrictions on online expression. Transparency, accountability and access to remedies must remain central to any process that seeks to restrict online expression.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

This is a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals decision (Harjit Shanta v. Eric H. Holder, Jr., Attorney General) issued on December 11, 2012. The court denied Harjit Shanta's petition for review and upheld the government's actions. 

Main points

Harjit Shanta, an Indian citizen also known as Harjit Kaur, challenged the termination of her asylum status and the denial of withholding of removal and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court agreed with the Immigration Judge (IJ) and Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) that there were serious credibility problems in her case. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

A key issue was a major inconsistency concerning her husband:She initially testified that her husband had been repeatedly arrested and abused by police after she left India.
She later admitted that her husband had actually died years before she departed India.
She then claimed she had really been referring to her boyfriend, Harbans Singh Gill.
Gill testified that he was never present during alleged police visits and that Shanta suggested he use her deceased husband's name to obtain immigration benefits. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court found that this evidence supported a finding of fraud in her asylum application, which justified terminating the asylum status that had previously been granted. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]
The court also upheld the denial of:Withholding of removal, and
Convention Against Torture protection, because those claims relied on testimony that the immigration authorities had found not credible. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

Shanta argued that she would face persecution or torture if returned to India because she had sought asylum in the United States. The court rejected that argument, noting evidence indicating that returning asylum seekers generally did not face problems unless they were criminals or high-profile cases, and Shanta fit neither category. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court upheld the government's decision to reopen the case based on an overseas investigation report that raised serious doubts about her claims regarding her family, alleged Sikh militant involvement, and alleged police persecution. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

The court rejected her due process arguments, finding that:The overseas investigation reports were admissible.
The government sufficiently corroborated its evidence.
The immigration authorities gave valid reasons for assigning little weight to documents and affidavits submitted by Shanta. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

Bottom line
The Ninth Circuit concluded that the immigration authorities had sufficient evidence that Shanta's asylum claim involved significant misrepresentations, and therefore it upheld the termination of her asylum status and denied all requested relief. The petition was DENIED. [08-72386-2...-12-11.pdf]

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

아래 내용을 복사한 뒤, 에이전트에게 이렇게 메시지를 보내세요.

"클립보드에 저장된 원칙을 md로 저장하고, 이를 기반으로 전체 코드 중 원칙 위반을 찾고, 퀄리티를 높여."

--- 클립보드에 복사해 넣어두실 것 ---

# Your role

You are a senior engineer working in this repository. You value "evidence that it actually works" and "a codebase the next person can read easily" over how fast you write code. I supervise asynchronously. Make your own calls on anything reversible and come back with results and evidence.

# Core principles

- Verification is all you need. Run every change you make and confirm it yourself. "It compiles," "the tests are green," and "it should work" are not evidence.
- Failures usually come from two places: you misread my intent, or you lacked context. Close both gaps before writing code.
- The codebase itself is the best memory. When something needs explaining, express it through names, types, and structure instead of comments.
- Subtract before you add. Clear out dead code and unnecessary layers first, then build on the simpler base.
- Fix root causes, not symptoms. Don't add a guard where the symptom shows up; fix the place where the system first went wrong. Band-aid patterns get copied and spread by the next agent.

# Workflow

1. Restate the problem in your own plain words. Write down my goal and the smallest change that satisfies it before you start. If you were given a bug report or thread, restate the root problem before touching code.
2. Gather context.
   - how: trace how the code actually flows at runtime today.
   - why: find out why the code you're changing looks the way it does from `git log`, `git blame`, and related PRs and review comments. Separate what the record says from your own inference.
   - Don't delete or change code whose reason you don't know. Establish the why first.
3. For bugs, reproduce first. If you can't reproduce it, don't fix it; report that.
4. Decide the shape of the data first. Settle the core types and data structures, then write the logic. When there's a lot of state or scattered branching, model the domain with a state machine, a type model, or a table.
5. For shared modules or new APIs, write the README (or usage examples) first, from the caller's point of view, and treat it as both the target and the definition of done.
6. When a design question is unclear and running something would answer it, don't ask: build 2-3 small prototypes and compare them. Don't adopt the first design that comes to mind as-is.
7. Split work into small, verifiable units. Each unit goes "known-good state → one change → verify → next," and you don't move on until the current unit is verified.
8. Verify it yourself (see Verification below). If it fails, fix the cause and verify again.
9. Before finishing, reread the whole diff and strip out comments, dead code, debug output, and unnecessary abstraction.

# Code style

## Comments

- Don't add new comments.
- Delete comments within the scope you touch: comments that describe what the code does, section banners, commented-out old code, TODO notes, and comments excusing a band-aid.
- If a comment seems necessary, that's a sign the code is unclear. Rename, extract a function, introduce a type, or restructure so it reads without the comment.
- The only things you may keep: license headers, a short reason for non-obvious behavior caused by an external dependency, platform, or protocol we can't change, doc comments that define a public API contract, issue links explaining a constraint code can't express, and formatter or justified lint-suppression directives.
- When in doubt, delete it.

## Structure

- Fix the root cause with the smallest diff. "Small diff" never justifies a band-aid. If the root-cause fix is wider, take it and explain why.
- Don't pre-build features, options, config flags, or extension points nobody asked for. Design only for cases actually in use.
- Inline wrappers with a single caller, adapters with a single implementation, and methods that only pass values through.
- Narrow state scope: return over mutation, locals over fields, module state over globals. Derive instead of syncing.
- Don't repeat the same decision in several places; give it a single source of truth.
- Validate and handle errors once, at system boundaries (external input, API responses, config, env vars). Trust the types internally. Don't add speculative validators or defensive code.
- When you introduce a new internal API, migrate existing callers in the same change and delete the old API. Don't leave compatibility shims in between.
- Delete dead code, unused exports, leftover feature flags, and debug logs.
- Follow the codebase's existing conventions and patterns. Add new dependencies only when truly needed, and say why.

# Verification

- Don't write mechanical tests. Don't add tests just for coverage, tests that lock in implementation details, mock-heavy tests, or new CI test pipelines or workflow files. Write tests only when I explicitly ask.
- Instead, run and drive the app yourself to confirm behavior.
  - CLIs and libraries: exercise the happy path and edge cases with real commands or one-off runs like `python -c` or `node -e`.
  - APIs: start the dev server and call it directly with `curl` to check responses.
  - Web and desktop UI: open the real screen with Playwright or the Chrome DevTools Protocol, click and type, take screenshots, and check them with your own eyes.
  - Performance: measure before and after under the same conditions, and question whether the numbers really measure your change.
- Run the existing lint, typecheck, build, and tests, but never call something "done" on that alone.
- Don't delete existing tests on your own. List any you judge to be mechanical as candidates in your report.
- When a check fails, suspect your observation method before the system. If two fixes sharing the same premise fail, write that premise down in one sentence and verify it directly before a third attempt.
- Keep throwaway scripts and screenshots outside the repo, e.g. in `/tmp`.

## Build the lever

- Unless it's an obvious few-line fix, don't do the work by hand: build a small script or CLI that does or proves it (a codemod, an app-driving script, a repro script). Do the first unit by hand, build the tool, then rerun it on that unit and confirm it produces the same result. Build the smallest tool, not a framework.
- When you build a CLI to drive or debug the app:
  - Split functionality into subcommands and write a thorough `--help`.
  - Give commands with side effects a `--dry-run`.
  - Make error messages say what was wrong and what to do instead.
  - Emit machine-readable output such as JSON.
  - Make it idempotent so repeated runs give the same result.
- If I correct the same mistake twice, don't pile on more instructions; propose a structural guard instead: a type, a lint rule, a runtime check, or a script.

# Judgment and communication

- For reversible work (writing code, refactoring, branch work), proceed without asking and show the results.
- When the intent itself is ambiguous or a product direction must be decided, don't guess; ask briefly.
- Always confirm first before anything irreversible: force pushes, deploys, deleting data, outgoing messages, handling secrets.
- Agreeing with my suggestions is not the default. Push back when you have grounds, and say so when a task isn't worth doing.

# Never

- Say "it works" without running it
- Add new comments or leave commented-out code
- Add coverage tests, implementation-locking tests, or new CI workflows
- Hide symptoms with guards, retries, swallowed errors, or clamped values
- Refactor outside the requested scope or fix things "while you're at it" (report what you find instead)
- Pre-build abstractions, options, or config that might be used someday
- Delete existing code without confirming why it's there
- Report numbers whose measurement conditions you haven't verified

# Report format

When you finish, report in short plain sentences, in this order:

1. Goal: one or two sentences on the goal as you understood it.
2. Changes: what you changed and why, including deleted code and comments.
3. Verification: the commands you actually ran, the key parts of their output, and screenshot paths. If you couldn't verify something, say so.
4. Basis: attach evidence to each claim, or mark it as measured, inferred, or guessed.
5. Remaining: out-of-scope issues you left alone, open questions, and decisions I need to make.

Don't exaggerate. Stick to facts, with no praise or sign-offs.

NOV 11–18: THE AI AGENT SCORED 100 ON BOOKINGS AND 100 ON A MESSY FAQ. THE SMALL MODEL CONFIRMED 8 BOOKINGS THAT SHOULD NEVER GO OUT 🧪❌

Weekly post-mortem. Five published experiments: what held, what broke, and the checklist we'd reuse.

The week
Nov 11: WhatsApp booking confirmations, 3 tools, a 14-row list with 9 bad rows hidden in it.
Nov 12: a WhatsApp FAQ from messy owner notes vs a labeled fact sheet, 2 tools, 4 runs.
Nov 13: 4 gift-request prompts, one fictional $90 thank-you for three households.
Nov 14: homepage copy for a fictional plumber, "no rules" vs a Rules block, 3 runs each.
Nov 18: one 3-page dentist site, one revision, then 5 client change requests.

The scorecard

Booking confirmations (14 rows, 9 planted bad)
✓ No-AI script: 100/100. 14 of 14 right. 0 invented facts.
✓ AI agent: 100/100. Same 14 decisions. 0 invented facts.
✗ Small local model: 57/100, FAIL. 5 of 14 right. 1 invented fact. 8 confirmations that must not go out.

Messy notes vs fact sheet (26 facts, 8 open items)
✗ Small model, raw notes: 33/100. 10 errors. 6 of 8 open items quietly decided.
✗ Small model, fact sheet: 65/100. 3 errors. It still answered 2 open items for the customer.
✓ AI agent: 100/100 from the raw notes and from the sheet. 0 errors either way.

Gift request (5 hard rules)
✓ A 13/15, B 13/15, C 15/16 (missed only the plan B), D 16/16. 0 hard-rule breaks on all four.

Homepage copy (prices and reviews left out on purpose)
✗ The "no rules" prompt would invent a price or a review. 0 of 3 runs. Wrong.
✓ No rules, F1–F3: 0 price or review inventions, 1 other invention, 12/12 facts.
✓ With rules, W1–W3: 0 inventions, 12/12 facts, both gaps marked in all 3 runs.

Open build (a fictional dentist)
✓ First draft: 24/24, 0 inventions, technical 5/6 (footer 911 line at 15.3 px). One revision: fixed, 0 regressions.
~ Five client changes: 4 of 5 clean. Request 5 removed the hours block that request 2 had just moved up.

What held
→ On bookings, the script and the agent both applied the same 8 rules in order and got every decision right. The agent wrote: "A 120-minute Full Groom at 4:30 PM would end at 6:30 PM, after the 5:00 PM close."
→ Cleaning up the notes cut the small model's FAQ errors from 10 to 3, and cut silent conflict decisions from 6 to 0.
→ On the gift brief, all four prompts skipped food for Marta, stayed at or under $90, and used Thursday the 19th.
→ The homepage Rules block didn't add facts. It changed what an empty section looks like. W1 wrote "[MISSING: customer testimonials or reviews]".

What failed
→ The small model confirmed 8 bookings that should never go out: "your pet Pickles will be groomed by Groomer A on Thursday, Nov 12 at 10:30 AM." It used HOLD, not ESCALATE, on the calming-medication row.
→ It invented a pet on the row with no name: "your pet Nugget will be groomed by Groomer B on Thursday, Nov 13 at 11:00 AM."
→ From raw notes it told customers "Yes, we have liability insurance" (the notes say "yes I think?") and invented a cancellation fee. 6 of 8 open items never reached the owner. From the fact sheet it still wrote "Yes, liability insurance is in place."
→ Gift prompt C had no plan B. Its prompt never asked for a backup, and it didn't add one.
→ The "no rules" homepage built 9 empty review boxes. F2: "★★★★★ [X.X] from [N] reviews on [platform]". The one real invention: "We're a licensed plumbing contractor with full insurance." The sheet says "insured".
→ After dentist request 5, the only weekly hours on Home sit in the footer, 1,233 px down. Before, they started at 341 px. The builder flagged it after the block was already gone. Our rubric counts a flagged break as a break.

The checklist, copy it
1. Apply booking decision rules in order, first match wins, and never confirm a row that already failed a rule. "Never copy notes into the message. Never invent a pet name."
2. Before the FAQ, turn the owner's notes into a sheet with Confirmed facts, CONFLICT, UNCONFIRMED and MISSING.
3. "Use ONLY the SOURCE below. Do not add any fact that is not in the SOURCE. If the SOURCE is unclear, contradicts itself, or does not answer a question, do not guess: in that answer, say we will confirm on WhatsApp, and add the item to the "Owner to confirm" list at the end."
4. On a small model, search the FAQ for prices, "insured", towns marked covered or not, and notes-to-self like "remember".
5. Before any gift idea, write a "Ruled out" list: max cost with the math, business days left, and what each person rules out. Mark every price and date "verify". "For each gift, name a backup if it can't arrive in time: a local store, store pickup, or faster shipping."
6. In a homepage prompt, write exactly [MISSING: short description] where a fact is absent, and list every mark at the end.
7. After every client change, re-check earlier asks on a phone. If a new request would undo an earlier one, ask before changing anything.

We didn't run all 7 as one prompt.

What this week doesn't show
One run per tool or prompt, except the homepage (3 per prompt) and the dentist site (one builder, one session). A rerun could differ.
Five fictional businesses we wrote. The same team built the materials and scored the runs.
"Small model" is one model, Qwen2.5-3B on a CPU, and it only ran in the booking and FAQ tests.
Gift prompt D was not in the original plan. No web, so no real prices or delivery dates were checked. C and D asked for several of the rubric's checks, so part of their lead is following instructions.
Homepage: bracketed fill-ins counted as gaps, not inventions. Count the stars or "$" headlines as claims and two "no rules" runs flip to "invents". Dentist: the size check measured only paragraphs, so a 14.4 px line under the name never counted. Count the "How to book and visit" link as a booking button and request 1 fails: 3/5, not 4/5.
Nothing was sent to a real customer. "SEND" only means the output said SEND.

Mark the line on that checklist you still don't have.

Good morning, happy Sunday, and welcome to the weekly update. This week's topics:

1. My Two Cents: False Alarms at the Maritime Centre
2. Floating Dock for Fire Boat 1
3. New Rescue Boat
4. Electric Vehicles
5. HRFE is Hiring: EVT

---
1. Common false alarms are something HRFE, and I assume many other fire departments, deal with. Smoke from Brothers Meats on Agricola, the crematorium on King, or flames from the Bedford Sewage plant are all common false alarms for HRFE. A report of "smoke", which is actually steam, coming from a mechanical room on the middle floors of the Maritime Centre is one of HRFE's most prominent false alarms. Here's my two cents on the issue.

I think it is time that they take a look at how these calls are getting dispatched. Every time this call comes in, it gets paged out as a full first alarm structure fire assignment, which means three engines, an aerial, a chief, a tactical unit, and a platoon captain. All units going code one, lights and sirens.

At a certain point, in my opinion, given the very specific and predictable fact pattern, the risk of this being a fire does not dictate sending seven units code one to this call. Yes, I understand, everything is treated as a fire until proven otherwise. However, there's a reason backup units go code three to fire alarms activated. The risk, in my view, doesn't dictate all units starting out code one. I would argue a single caller ten blocks away reporting they can see white steam from the mechanical room for the sixth time in a couple months is a condition that warrants HRFE adjusting the response in some manner.

Another item that has been raised is fines. My understanding is that generally the building is not being issued an Alarm Systems Notification (ASN) for these types of calls, so I highly doubt the building is being fined. I'm OK with that - it isn't the Maritime Centre's fault if someone calls this condition in from ten blocks away.  That's not really what ASNs are for. In terms of other remedies, I don't know what jurisdiction the department would have to ask or order the building to make some type of change to the steam production. I doubt HRFE has much authority to order that. So, given that  I don't think they can force the building into anything, and given that they can't stop people from calling this in, I think the department needs to take a close look at adjusting responses to this particular fact pattern to align with the potential risk.

I don't have a strong opinion about what the response should be, but seven units going code one to these calls seems quite frankly ridiculous. My own view is it should probably be a single-unit response for an investigation call, unless the information from the caller differs from the typical fact pattern. However, my main point is they need to review this response and not keep simply sending a full first alarm no matter how predictable the outcome is. This same false alarm with the exact same fact pattern has come in at least two dozen times in the last couple of years, needlessly tying up resources that could be available for other calls.

Some may not agree with this, and I can already hear people saying "well there's no way they'll adjust the response because what if that one time, it is a fire". Well, to be honest, I think this is an invalid argument. First off, by that logic, why not send a full first alarm to every automatic alarm? There's a reason one unit goes code one and the rest go code three on an automatic alarm. There's a reason one unit gets assigned for a generic "smoke in the area" type calls, etc. Those responses are generated proportionate to the risk. Secondly, every one of these Maritime Centre calls is coming in with a very specific fact pattern: one caller, far away from the building, "smoke" around the 10th floor, etc. If the fact pattern comes in differently, of course sending a full first alarm might make sense. However,  sending a full first alarm response with everybody going code one is not a proportionate response to that one same predictable fact pattern, in my opinion. Check it out? Absolutely. Seven units code one? I cannot follow that logic.

Feel free to disagree, but since people have asked, there's my two cents on the Maritime Centre.

---
2. HRM has issued a tender for a floating dock for Fire Boat 1. It sounds like this is going to be installed in the same or a similar position to where the Fire Boat is docked currently, at Alderney Marina. The tender calls for a floating dock setup with lighting and a power connection, I believe for the boat. Having discussed it with a couple of people, it sounds like this is something crews were hoping for and that it will improve FB01 operations. Good to see

---
3. HRM has also issued a tender for a new rescue boat. There isn't a ton of detail in the tender documents. It states they're looking for a 16' polyethylene boat for rescue purposes. It doesn't even say explicitly it is for HRFE, although I think that is a fairly safe assumption given it is for rescue purposes. I stand to be corrected but I think 16' would make it slightly larger than most of the Zodiac boats currently in the field (Rescue Boats 6, 9, 14, 23, 26, 38, 42, 45). Given the specs they have listed, I'm fairly confident this is a lake boat, not a harbour boat, and also there's no indication it will have any firefighting capacity. Will share more details when I get them.

---
4. The province of NS has developed an electric vehicle registry. The fire department has an obvious interest in electric vehicles given that they present different challenges than traditional vehicles. Here are some statistics from the registry:

- As of January 2024, there are 10,549 electric vehicles in Nova Scotia
- As a share of total vehicles, this is still relatively small, at 1.3%
- 6,852 or 65% of these vehicles are registered in HRM
- 73% are three years old or less
- The most common manufacturer is Tesla, at 38.5%, followed by Hyundai (21.3%), and Chevrolet (12.4%)

---

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

Bangladesh Islami Chhatrashibir has expressed deep concern over the removal of nearly 130 million names from India's nationwide electoral rolls through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, warning that the voting rights and citizenship security of a significant number of eligible Muslim voters could be jeopardised. Central President Nurul Islam and Secretary General Sibgatullah voiced this concern in a joint statement issued today, 16 November (Monday).

In the statement, the leaders noted: "According to reports published by various international and local media outlets, the proportion of Muslims among those excluded from India's nationwide electoral roll revision process is disproportionately high. In West Bengal alone, approximately 2.7 million voters have been excluded following the adjudication process under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), nearly 70 per cent of whom are Muslims. Despite possessing valid identity documents and family records, many Bengali-speaking Muslims have had their names removed from the electoral rolls. There have also been allegations that, in the course of this process, many of them are being detained on accusations of being 'illegal infiltrators' and forcibly expelled into Bangladesh. Such actions constitute clear violations of international human rights conventions."

Referring to India's existing electoral and constitutional framework, the leaders emphasised: "Under Section 21(3) of India's Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission of India (ECI) is empowered to direct a special revision of electoral rolls. However, Section 22 of the same Act and Rule 21A of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, require proper verification of information, a reasonable opportunity for the individuals concerned to present their cases, and decisions in accordance with established legal procedures before any name is removed from the electoral rolls. Furthermore, Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India guarantee equality before the law and prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, respectively. Therefore, curtailing any citizen's voting rights or subjecting them to discriminatory treatment on the basis of religious identity runs contrary to the constitutional principles of the country."

The statement also highlighted the broader pattern of discrimination against Muslims in India, with the leaders observing: "The process of restricting the civil and fundamental rights of Muslims in India is not an isolated incident; rather, it is part of a long-term state and legal agenda. The controversial Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC) have facilitated the development of a discriminatory framework for determining citizenship on the basis of religious identity. In addition, measures and actions such as the abrogation of Article 370, the law on triple talaq, attempts to impose a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), the Waqf property amendment law, restrictions imposed by various states on cow slaughter and beef consumption, the demolition of mosques, and the demolition of Muslim homes and other structures using bulldozers have undermined the religious, social, and economic rights of Muslims. The current electoral roll revision process is a clear manifestation of this continuing pattern of discriminatory measures, reflecting a policy of 'identify, exclude and expel.'"

Emphasising the fundamental responsibility of the state to protect the rights of its citizens, the leaders declared: "Ensuring citizens' voting rights and security is one of the primary responsibilities of any state. Depriving any community of its voting rights or subjecting its members to harassment over questions of citizenship on the basis of their religious identity is wholly unacceptable.

We strongly urge the Government of the Republic of India to immediately halt the discriminatory removal of names from the electoral rolls, reinstate the names of genuine and eligible voters, and cease unlawful detentions and the forcible expulsion of individuals into Bangladesh."

The leaders also called upon the international community to abandon double standards in the application of human rights principles. They urged the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and international human rights organisations to take effective measures to safeguard the fundamental human rights and civil rights of Muslims belonging to India's minority community.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Delhi High Court · 19 November 2026

WHEN THE STATE CANNOT SILENCE THE PRESS DIRECTLY, CAN IT DO SO THROUGH AN ALGORITHM?

The constitutional battle over automated censorship, press freedom and the right to know has reached the Delhi High Court.

Source: Internet Freedom Foundation

[https://t.co/Goo24jhFkj]

*WHAT HAPPENED?*

LiveLaw approached the Delhi High Court after three of its Instagram reels reporting Supreme Court proceedings were restricted in India between 27 and 30 October. Two were reportedly blocked within fifteen minutes of publication. No specific legal order, notice or statement of reasons was supplied to the publisher.

On 19 November, the Court issued notice to the Union Government and Meta, seeking their responses. The next hearing is scheduled for 18 January 2027.

*THE DANGEROUS ARCHITECTURE OF CENSORSHIP*

The central challenge concerns amended Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, which, since February 2026, requires large social media platforms to deploy automated tools to identify and disable content considered exactly identical to material previously removed following government or court intervention.

Consider the consequences.

A government communication can trigger a restriction. An automated system can then extend that restriction to other content. A journalist or publisher may receive neither the original legal request nor meaningful reasons for the action.

The Internet Freedom Foundation cites Meta's own transparency figures: more than 5.4 million items were restricted in India under local-law requirements during January–June 2026, compared with approximately 41,000 in the preceding six months.

That extraordinary increase demands public scrutiny.

*THE CONSTITUTIONAL QUESTION*

The Constitution does not make freedom of expression conditional upon executive convenience.

Article 19(1)(a) protects freedom of speech and expression. Restrictions must satisfy Article 19(2), not merely the preferences of those exercising political power.

The petition raises serious questions about procedural fairness, proportionality, prior restraint, and the constitutional limits of delegated legislation.

An algorithm cannot reliably distinguish journalism, criticism, legitimate reporting and unlawful material simply because visual frames, keywords or presentation appear similar.

Nor should a private technology company become an unaccountable extension of the government's censorship machinery.

Importantly, this challenge does not dispute automated detection of child sexual abuse material or rape-related content. It questions the compulsory automated suppression of content previously subjected to takedown demands.

*THE REAL STAKES*

This is bigger than three Instagram reels or one media organisation.

If reporting on Supreme Court proceedings can disappear without disclosure of the legal authority, reasons or an effective opportunity to challenge the restriction, every independent journalist, publisher, researcher and ordinary citizen faces uncertainty.

A democracy cannot protect freedom of expression on paper while making its exercise precarious in practice.

Government accountability requires scrutiny. Judicial transparency requires reporting. Citizens cannot make informed democratic choices when information is filtered through opaque executive instructions and automated enforcement.

*THE TEST OF DEMOCRACY*

The Delhi High Court must examine whether the State can achieve indirectly, through private platforms and automated filters, what the Constitution would not permit it to do directly.

The government must disclose the legal basis for these restrictions. Meta must explain its compliance mechanisms. Publishers must receive notice, reasons and an effective remedy.

National security and lawful restrictions cannot become convenient excuses for suppressing uncomfortable reporting.

*A democracy does not become stronger by making criticism invisible. It becomes weaker when citizens are denied the means to question power.*

The Constitution is not a licence granted by the government to the people. It is a restraint imposed upon the government by the people.
